Ministers are in denial about the scale of the crises we face
article.full_text: This (Just 20 of 6,600 Defra staff working on climate adaptation amid drought and wildfires, 12 August) is a shocking revelation from a government that has repeatedly assured us it understands the risk of the breakdown of nature and climate. Clearly not. Families forced to deal with school closures, hospitals having to cancel appointments, wildfires continuing to tear through the country, and, so far, more than 2,700 deaths recorded from extreme heat. And yet adaptation remains a tiny corner of one department. It’s not as though ministers haven’t been warned. The Climate Change Committee raises the alarm in every progress report it produces, urging the government to act. So what’s gone wrong? Have the impacts of ecosystem collapse and climate change become politically expendable to the government? From a war on those pesky newts and bats to Andy Burnham’s endless game of ‘“will he, won’t he” over more oil and gas, this is Westminster fanning the flames of climate change. The communities facing firewaves, floods and extreme drought don’t want to hear what’s already taking place – they want to know what’s going to change. Saying that we’re “already acting” clearly does not match the scale of the crisis. Just ask the “UK’s first climate evacuees” on whom you reported in February. Climate adaptation is a whole-of-government problem, not just for one desk at Defra. Why is there an AI minister around the Cabinet table, but no resilience and adaptation minister? Why don’t we have a dedicated commissioner with the authority to ensure that departments prepare for the risks of climate and nature breakdown, and to make sure that there is a public face for these issues so that communities are protected? And, crucially, why is no one asking these questions in government? Dr Amy McDonnell Co-executive director, Zero Hour • Have an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? ‘She’s not afraid of anyone’: the prison writings of one of Hong Kong’s last outspoken democracy activists
article.full_text: In one essay written from prison, Chow Hang-tung worries about her hairstyle before court appearances because there are no combs or mirrors in her cell. “In a place like prison, where anything that is personal is stripped away, it’s even more important to hold on to every means by which you can express yourself,” she writes. “Don’t let uniform, depersonalised rules, dress codes, schedules, and behavioural requirements grind down your edges and mould you into a ‘model citizen’”. The vignette is everyday, almost mundane. It stands in contrast to Chow’s position as one of Hong Kong’s most outspoken dissidents, one who has been detained for nearly five years awaiting trial over her role in organising an annual vigil marking the Tiananmen Square massacre. Her case represents one of the last high-profile national security trials to be heard in Hong Kong, as the national security law imposed by Beijing in 2020 extinguishes what was once one of the world’s most widely watched pro-democracy struggles. On Friday, Chow and her co-defendant Lee Cheuk-yan were found guilty of “incitement to subversion” by a Hong Kong court. They face a maximum penalty of 10 years in jail when they are sentenced later in the year. As the years pass by, the 41-year-old barrister has written screeds from behind bars on everything from the meaning of freedom to the legacy of the 1989 massacre, some of which have been translated by Brian Kern, a writer and human rights activist. Chow’s profile has only grown since she has been detained. She has won several human rights awards, and her social media profiles, which are managed on her behalf, are regularly updated with her writings from prison. In another essay, she describes being handed a white Mickey Mouse t-shirt to wear in court because she is not allowed to wear clothing that carries the branding of her protest group, the Hong Kong Alliance. “The Mickey Mouse t-shirt may seem innocent on the surface, but isn’t it still a prison uniform provided by the correctional facility? Even before the Alliance has been convicted, its clothes have already become contraband,” she writes. While some writings are breezy and irreverent, many are deeply considered essays on defending civil rights in the face of a powerful and oppressive Chinese Communist party. As a highly regarded barrister who has been representing herself in court, she also dives into legal philosophy. “She’s not afraid of anything or anyone,” said Kevin Yam, a Hong Kong lawyer who now lives in exile. “For a lot of us who are outside Hong Kong now and sometimes feel a bit dispirited by things, her example and her inspiration is a big factor in us not losing hope and keeping our spirits up.” Wu Yangwei, Chow’s fiance, a Chinese activist better known by his pen name, Ye Du, said it was Chow’s interest in mainland Chinese struggles that first attracted him to her. “From the moment I met her… I felt that she was incredibly innocent, deeply compassionate, and deeply empathetic toward China’s democracy and human rights defense movements,” Wu said. He now lives under close police surveillance in Guangdong province. ‘A society that loses freedom of speech … loses its very soul’ Chow was arrested in September 2021 along with two other organisers of the now disbanded Hong Kong Alliance in Support of Democratic Movements of China. The Hong Kong Alliance’s annual Tiananmen vigil, which attracted tens of thousands of Hongkongers each year, was banned in 2020 on the grounds of pandemic control. Chow, along with Lee Cheuk-yan and Albert Ho, were charged with incitement to subversion under Hong Kong’s new sweeping national security law. Chow and Lee pleaded not guilty in their trial, which ended on 19 May, while Ho submitted a guilty plea, which could help him get a sentence reduction.
